newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD wants monetary union on time in 1999.
newsitem.headline: German SPD wants monetary union on time in 1999.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democratic party (SPD) wants the creation of a single European currency to go ahead according to plan in 1999, party chief Oskar Lafontaine said on Monday.
Lafontaine told a conference of the SPD's youth wing that fluctuations in Europe's currency rates had exacerbated the continent's unemployment crisis.
"European governments must take the Maastricht treaty seriously and coordinate their economic policies more strongly to fight unemployment together," Lafontaine said.
The SPD has not always stood behind monetary union -- it lost votes in regional polls earlier this year when it campaigned on a Eurosceptic platform. Germany faces parliamentary polls in 1998.

While agreeing that the entry criteria outlined in Maastricht should be met, the SPD has been at loggerheads with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party governing coalition over how to cut spending to achieve those goals.
The SPD has staunchly opposed government welfare cuts, while calling for more savings in the defence budget. It is also trying to block the abolition of wealth taxes in this year's tax bill.

Lafontaine called on the Bundesbank and other European central banks to pursue more growth-oriented policies. He also said a European job-creation pact was needed and the Maastricht social chapter should be fully implemented.
